source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple choice and true/false when the format is right. A model can score its own sample as P(True). It can also be trained to predict P(IK), whether it knows the answer. This is the base paper for stated vs actual confidence.
numbers: 52B model. Calibration improves with size and from 0-shot to few-shot. P(True) generalises across five sampling tasks (TriviaQA, Lambada, Arithmetic, GSM8k, Codex). P(IK) is trained on TriviaQA, partly transfers, but is poorly calibrated on new tasks.
quote: larger models are well-calibrated on diverse multiple choice and true/false questions when they are provided in the right format
limits: Mostly logit-based (token probabilities), not words. Calibration is weaker zero-shot. Only models up to 52B, from before 2023.
agent_relevance: Confidence from a second pass over our own sample (P(True)) is a usable check. Do not trust it on a new task type without a held-out calibration set (G3).

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) RLHF section (3.3)
finding: RLHF policies look very badly calibrated on log-probabilities, but one temperature change largely repairs it. So miscalibration of RLHF models can be a scale problem, not lost information.
numbers: 52B helpful-and-harmless RLHF policy. Setting temperature T=2.5 largely fixes calibration curves on MMLU, MMLU true/false and TruthfulQA (5-shot).
limits: Applies to token probabilities, not verbalized numbers. Verbalized confidence of RLHF models is a different channel (see Leng 2024, Tian 2023).
agent_relevance: Do not read RLHF overconfidence as total loss of signal. Rank information may survive even when levels are wrong. Use confidence by rank, not by raw level.

source: Lin, Hilton & Evans (2022) Teaching Models to Express Their Uncertainty in Words
finding: First demonstration that a model (GPT-3 175B) can be finetuned to say '61%' or 'medium' about its own answer, with calibration that holds under distribution shift. The model was sensitive to its own uncertainty, not just copying human examples.
numbers: CalibratedMath: 21 arithmetic tasks. Finetuned on Add-subtract (median accuracy 21%), tested on Multi-answer (median accuracy 65%) and Multiply-divide. Verbalized probability beat the zero-shot answer logit and matched the indirect logit under shift. Meaningless label words worked slightly better than words like 'lowest'.
quote: the model also remains moderately calibrated under distribution shift, and is sensitive to uncertainty in its own answers, rather than imitating human examples
limits: Needs finetuning on about 100 graded questions per sub-task. Arithmetic only. The Multiply-divide shift is small so a constant baseline does well there. Prompt-only verbalization was not the main result.
agent_relevance: Origin of the stated-confidence idea. A scaffold cannot finetune, so the lesson is that calibration comes from graded outcomes. Our agent could keep a running record of its own hits and misses.

source: Mielke, Szlam, Dinan & Boureau (2022) Reducing Conversational Agents' Overconfidence Through Linguistic Calibration
finding: Chit-chat models (BlenderBot family) answer TriviaQA questions with confident wording even when wrong. A separate calibrator predicts the chance of being right. A controllable generator then adds hedges to match. This is the first calibrator-plus-controlled-wording pipeline and a direct ancestor of verbalized confidence work.
numbers: Vanilla BST 2.7B: accuracy 4.8% on TriviaQA validation; it answers 29.45% of test questions confidently while only 14% of those confident answers are correct. After the calibrator-controlled pipeline, correctness of confident answers rose from 13.7% to 38.9%, by answering fewer questions confidently.
limits: Small 2021-era chatbots with very low accuracy. Needs a trained calibrator. Human judging of correctness. Not an instruction-tuned LLM.
agent_relevance: A design our agent can copy: keep the confidence estimator separate from the writer, and let code map the estimate to wording (G12 style). Also shows the cost: fewer confident answers.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration: Strategies for Eliciting Calibrated Confidence Scores from RLHF-LMs
finding: For RLHF chat models, asking for a probability in words often gives better calibration than the model's own token probabilities. Asking for several guesses with a probability each helps further. Chain of thought did not help verbalized calibration.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4, Claude 1/2, Llama-2-70B-chat on TriviaQA, SciQ, TruthfulQA. gpt-3.5 ECE TriviaQA: label prob 0.140 vs verbalized 1-stage top-1 0.068 (top-2 0.050). SciQ: 0.256 vs 0.234 (top-4 0.065). TruthfulQA: 0.451 vs 0.389 (top-4 0.203). gpt-4 TriviaQA ECE 0.078 vs 0.024. Headline: relative ECE cut of over 50% in many cells.
quote: verbalized confidences emitted as output tokens are typically better-calibrated than the model's conditional probabilities
limits: Factual recall only. Large differences between model families: Claude 1 was weak at verbalizing, Llama-2-70B gave mixed gains. 1-stage and 2-stage prompts sometimes differ a lot. On TruthfulQA ECE stays high. AUC is about flat, so the gain is in level, not ranking.
agent_relevance: Practical recipe: ask for top-k guesses with a probability each, in one stage. Do not rely on CoT to fix confidence. Expect prompt sensitivity, so test the exact prompt.

source: Xiong et al. (2024, ICLR) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs
finding: Benchmark of prompts, sampling and aggregation for black-box confidence. Vanilla verbalized confidence is overconfident, clusters at 80-100% in multiples of 5, and mimics human talk about confidence. Scaling helps but is far from ideal. Human-inspired prompts help partly.
numbers: Five models (GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Vicuna, LLaMA 2-70B), eight tasks. Average ECE of vanilla verbalized confidence for GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and Vicuna is above 0.377. GPT-4 has lower ECE but average AUROC of only 62.7%. About 22.2% AUROC gain from GPT-3 to GPT-4. White-box vs black-box AUROC gap is small: 0.522 vs 0.605. Professional-knowledge tasks (law, ethics) stay hard.
quote: LLMs, when verbalizing their confidence, tend to be overconfident, potentially imitating human patterns of expressing confidence
limits: No method wins everywhere. ECE can drop just by saying 100% for everything: GPT-4 on GSM8K, accuracy 93.6%, ECE 0.064 with all samples at 100%, so no discrimination.
agent_relevance: Warns that a low ECE can be fake. A confidence guardrail must check discrimination (can it separate right from wrong), not only level.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) sampling and aggregation results
finding: Agreement across several sampled answers gives much better failure prediction than a single verbalized number. Mixing verbalized confidence into the consistency weight (Avg-Conf) gives the best AUROC. Pair-Rank (ask which of two answers is more likely) gives the lowest ECE.
numbers: GSM8K AUROC rose from 54.8% (single verbalized, near random) to 92.7% with 5 samples and consistency aggregation (GPT-4). Pair-Rank reached average ECE as low as 0.028; Avg-Conf had best AUROC on 5 of 6 datasets (GPT-4, Top-K prompt, self-random sampling). ECE and AUROC improve as samples go from M=1 to 13.
limits: Samples from one model are correlated, so consistency can be confidently wrong (our G4). Costs M times more calls. Gain is largest on arithmetic.
agent_relevance: Backs our rule that agreement is a hint. Verbalized confidence adds value mainly as a weight on agreement, not alone.

source: Yona, Aharoni & Geva (2024) Can LLMs Faithfully Express Their Intrinsic Uncertainty in Words?
finding: Defines faithful response uncertainty: the hedge in the text should match the model's own internal confidence, measured by answer consistency. Leading chat models fail: they answer decisively even when internally unsure, and prompting barely helps.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4-turbo, Gemini Nano/Pro/Ultra on PopQA and Natural Questions. cMFG (faithfulness, 0.5 = chance) for the Vanilla prompt is 0.52-0.57 for every model. Best non-vanilla cell: Gemini Ultra on PopQA with an Uncertainty instruction, 0.70. GPT-4-turbo reaches 0.63 on PopQA with Uncertainty+ but 0.57 on NQ. Models produced no uncertainty expressions under the vanilla prompt.
quote: State of the art models struggle at faithfully communicating uncertainty
limits: Measures match with intrinsic (sampling-consistency) confidence, not with correctness. Decisiveness scored by an LLM with a few-shot prompt; it agreed with human perception of hedge words in a 100-answer check.
agent_relevance: Wording in the output is a weak channel by default. If words must carry confidence, the program should write the words from a number it computed (G12), not trust the model's own hedges.

source: Zhou, Jurafsky & Hashimoto (2024) Relying on the Unreliable: The Impact of Language Models' Reluctance to Express Uncertainty
finding: Deployed models rarely hedge, and when told to state confidence they become overconfident. In human experiments, users rely on the output nearly as much with or without markers. Preference data used for alignment penalises hedged text, which may push RLHF toward overconfidence.
numbers: Nine models tested. Average 47% error among responses with expressions of certainty (about 53% correct, random 25%). Strengthener markers appear in about 20% of generations and weakeners in about 14% on average. Users rely on strengtheners and plain answers nearly 90% of the time; with weakeners about 90% choose to look the answer up. In preference datasets, texts with weakeners are chosen less often than strengthened ones (about 8-9% less).
limits: Human experiments on crowd workers with a trivia-like task. Marker use is partly prompt dependent. Effect of marker wording on reliance depends on whether the model is calibrated in the session.
agent_relevance: Stated confidence from chat models is inflated, and human-facing hedges change human behaviour. Our agent talks to a program, so we can avoid the human-bias channel.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025, Nature Machine Intelligence) What Large Language Models Know and What People Think They Know
finding: Calibration gap: people trust LLM answers more than the model's own confidence warrants when the model gives default explanations. Aligning explanation wording with the model's real confidence narrows the gap and the discrimination gap.
numbers: N=301 participants (284 retained), 40 questions each. Model AUC 0.751 (GPT-3.5, multiple choice), 0.746 (PaLM2), 0.781 (GPT-4o short answer). Human AUC with default explanations 0.589, 0.602, 0.592. Human confidence has much higher ECE than model confidence. Multiple choice: LLMs overconfident; short answer: slightly underconfident.
limits: US native-English crowd workers; trivia style questions. Tied to specific explanation styles.
agent_relevance: The model's internal confidence has real signal (AUC 0.75-0.78). The loss happens at the wording step. Supports computing confidence by code and rendering it plainly.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) explanation length experiment
finding: Longer explanations raise human confidence without raising accuracy. Uncertainty phrases such as 'I am not sure' move human confidence strongly in the right direction.
numbers: Low vs medium vs high confidence wording: Bayes factor above 100 in all three experiments. Long vs short explanation: BF=25 for higher confidence with long. Human AUC 0.54 (long) and 0.57 (uncertainty-only); BF=0.23, no gain in discrimination from extra length.
limits: Human perception only; the effect of length on an LLM reader was not tested.
agent_relevance: Fluent length reads as evidence. Our agent should not count a long justification as support for confidence. A similar verbosity bias is known for LLM judges.

source: Kim, Liao, Vorvoreanu, Ballard & Vaughan (2024) 'I'm Not Sure, But...': Uncertainty Expression and User Reliance
finding: Pre-registered human study (N=404) on medical questions with a fictional LLM search tool. First-person hedges ('I'm not sure, but...') lowered confidence and agreement with the system and raised accuracy. General-perspective hedges ('It's not clear, but...') had weaker, non-significant effects.
numbers: N=404 kept of 656 collected (38.4% excluded by 5 pre-registered criteria). Agreement with the system's answer: 80.9% in the control group with the AI vs 58.4% with no AI. Own internet search: 19.1% (control) vs 92.9% (no AI).
limits: Fictional system with scripted answers; crowd workers; medical questions only.
agent_relevance: Wording of confidence is a human-facing lever. For an agent-to-agent loop it matters less than how the number is computed.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know
finding: Prompting alone does not give good calibration. Finetuning on about 1,000 graded correct/incorrect answers (LoRA) beats prompt-based and sampling baselines, and the estimator works across tasks and even on other models' answers. Prompted confidence stays poor as base models improve.
numbers: On open-ended MMLU with LLaMA-2, LLaMA-3 and Mistral models, prompting methods have ECE that does not improve with model ability and AUROC that improves only slightly; even the best prompted model lags the worst finetuned one (LLaMA-2 7B). About 1,000 labeled examples are enough; 20,000 add little.
limits: Needs weights and graded data. A human user study shows uncertainty estimates change use of the LLM; details not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Argues against trusting a prompted number. A scaffold-only agent should treat stated confidence as a weak feature and calibrate it against graded outcomes in its own record.

source: Band et al. (2024) Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations
finding: Defines linguistic calibration for long text: confidence statements should let a reader make calibrated forecasts. Trains with an RL objective over the reader's downstream predictions, and improves calibration of long answers while keeping accuracy.
numbers: Abstract and introduction read: beats factuality-finetuned baselines at comparable accuracy; the effect carries to scientific and biomedical questions and a held-out biography task. Exact numbers not extracted this session.
limits: Training method; exact figures not recorded. Reader simulated by an LLM.
agent_relevance: The right target for a confidence statement is what a reader will do with it. For our agent the reader is the program that decides to stop, retry or ask.

source: Leng et al. (2025, ICLR) Taming Overconfidence in LLMs: Reward Calibration in RLHF
finding: RLHF makes models verbalize overconfidence. Reward models are biased toward high stated confidence regardless of answer quality. Two fixes (PPO-M: calibrated reward model; PPO-C: calibrated reward calculation) lower ECE without hurting accuracy.
numbers: Llama3-8B and Mistral-7B, six datasets. Vanilla PPO worsens ECE and AUC compared to SFT. PPO-M on Llama3-8B cuts ECE by 6.44 points and raises accuracy by 2.73 points on GSM8K. A DPO variant (CDPO) cuts ECE by over 50% in a reported setting.
limits: Small open models; confidence is elicited via a system prompt inserted in 25% of training prompts.
agent_relevance: Explains why chat models over-state confidence: it is trained in. A scaffold cannot remove that, so correct for it downstream.

source: Yang, Tsai & Yamada (2024/2026) On Verbalized Confidence Scores for LLMs
finding: Large benchmark of how to ask for verbalized confidence. Reliability depends strongly on the prompt. Well-calibrated scores are possible with some prompt methods. Models of 70B or more reach ECE near 0.1; the smallest model (gemma1.1-2b) is much worse. For tiny models a simple prompt change (probability score) helps most; few-shot and multi-guess ranking help less.
numbers: ECE about 0.1 for LLMs with at least 70B parameters (results text). Prompt variants compared: percentage 0-100%, decimal 0-1, and five discrete levels.
limits: Per-dataset numbers not extracted. Results depend on the exact prompt, so may not carry to new model versions.
agent_relevance: Pick the elicitation format by testing, and pin it. Changing the scale (percent vs decimal vs words) changes the quality.

source: Zeng, Xuan, Cui & Voigt (2025) Thinking Out Loud: Do Reasoning Models Know When They're Right?
finding: Reasoning-trace distillation and RL improve verbalized calibration on reasoning tasks in a ladder: instruct, then SFT reasoning, then RL reasoning. But reasoning models say I don't know much less on factuality benchmarks, which suggests weaker awareness of knowledge limits in small models. Confidence is higher when reasoning is shorter.
numbers: R1-Distill-Qwen-32B on AIME: accuracy 9.67% to 65.7%, ECE 0.752 to 0.240, AUROC 0.695 to 0.813. Beyond about 10,000 reasoning tokens, small models show a modest ECE rise; DeepSeek-R1 does not.
limits: Open models of several sizes. The reasoning tax is seen in small models only. Fewer than 1.5% of instances failed the format.
agent_relevance: Reasoning makes numbers better on reasoning tasks but not on knowledge limits. An abstain rule must not depend on the model saying I don't know.

source: Mei et al. (2025) Reasoning about Uncertainty: Do Reasoning Models Know When They Don't Know?
finding: Reasoning models are usually overconfident: stated confidence often above 85%, especially on wrong answers. They get more overconfident with deeper reasoning when accuracy does not rise. Self-review (introspective UQ) helps some models (o3-Mini, DeepSeek R1) and hurts Claude 3.7 Sonnet.
numbers: ECE strongly negatively correlated with accuracy across models (Gemini r=-1). On GPQA, going from low to high reasoning depth gave +10.8% accuracy and -5.5% ECE; on easier tasks (StrategyQA) calibration was unchanged. Claude was best calibrated by a wide margin. Introspection with medium or high prompts cut ECE on all three hard sets except one cell.
limits: Conflicts with Yoon 2025 on the effect of depth. Differences may come from datasets, models, or whether accuracy rises with depth. Introspection effects vary by dataset and prompt.
agent_relevance: Self-review of the reasoning chain is not a safe way to fix confidence: it is model-dependent (G2).

source: Yoon et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence
finding: Reasoning models with long chains of thought are better calibrated than their non-reasoning twins, and calibration gets better as the chain goes on. The gain comes from slow-thinking behaviours (exploring alternatives, backtracking). Removing them hurts calibration. Prompting non-reasoning models to slow-think helps.
numbers: Six reasoning models on six datasets: strictly better calibration than non-reasoning counterparts in 33 of 36 settings.
limits: Contradicts parts of Mei 2025 and Zeng 2025. Calibration still varies by task and model; the mechanism is shown with behavioural ablations only.
agent_relevance: A scaffold step that tries alternatives before stating confidence has some support, but it is a single-paper result. It fits G1: trigger on a signal, not by schedule.

source: Damani et al. (2026, ICLR) Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty (RLCR)
finding: Reward for correctness alone (RLVR) harms calibration. Adding a Brier-score term on the stated confidence (RLCR) keeps accuracy and gives much better calibration, in and out of domain. Confidence can also weight samples at test time.
numbers: HotpotQA: RLCR without analysis ECE 0.09 vs RLVR 0.37, accuracy 61.7% vs 63.0%, tokens 113 vs 92. Explicit uncertainty reasoning lowers Brier and ECE for both RLCR and RLVR. Proven: a bounded proper scoring rule makes accurate and calibrated models optimal.
limits: Training method; needs RL access. Models of 7-8B.
agent_relevance: Brier scoring of stated confidence works as a training signal. For our agent, the same score on a logged record can grade whether to trust the number.

source: Jang et al. (2025) Verbalized Confidence Triggers Self-Verification
finding: Finetuning with scalar self-consistency confidence labels alone makes a model write longer, self-checking answers for low-confidence questions and short ones for high-confidence. A rethink step at test time using the confidence improves accuracy.
numbers: Trained on GSM8K; tested on MATH-500 and ARC-Challenge. On ARC-Challenge, Llama improves accuracy by 6.3% and ECE by 71%; Qwen 9.1% higher accuracy and 33% better ECE.
limits: Small models (Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen); one training domain.
agent_relevance: Evidence for doubt on a signal: a low stated confidence can trigger extra checking (G1). In our case the program holds the threshold.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Are LLM Decisions Faithful to Verbal Confidence? (RiskEval)
finding: Models give calibrated-looking confidence but do not act on it. When wrong answers cost more, the models neither lower confidence nor abstain, so utility collapses.
numbers: Tested with penalties up to 100 per wrong answer on HLE, GPQA and GSM8K. Average utility falls sharply negative above moderate penalties on HLE and GPQA; models almost never abstain even when abstaining is optimal.
limits: Frontier models via API; verifiable benchmarks only.
agent_relevance: Direct support for a code-side decision rule: the program, not the model, compares confidence with the cost of error and decides to answer, retry, or abstain.

source: Kumaran et al. (2026, ICML) How do LLMs Compute Verbal Confidence?
finding: Mechanistic study. Confidence is not computed when it is asked for. It forms at answer-adjacent positions during answer generation, is cached, then read out. The cached signal explains variance in verbal confidence beyond token log-probabilities, so it looks like an answer-quality evaluation, not a fluency readout.
numbers: Gemma 3 27B (TriviaQA, BigMath, MMLU), Qwen 2.5 7B, Magistral Small 24B. Blocking attention from the confidence slot to question and answer tokens gave about 10% token change (control level); blocking its path to the post-answer position changed the token up to 21%; blocking that position's attention to answer tokens gave about 20% changes.
limits: Three open models only. Interpretability inference, not proof for closed models.
agent_relevance: Stated confidence reflects an internal assessment made while answering. This supports using it as a feature, and suggests the signal is there but gets lost in the wording.

source: Cacioli (2026) Verbal Confidence Saturation in 3-9B Open-Weight Instruction-Tuned LLMs (pre-registered)
finding: Small instruction-tuned models mostly output the top number. All seven failed a validity screen for item-level discrimination. Categorical elicitation did not rescue it and often wrecked the task.
numbers: 524 TriviaQA items, 8,384 deterministic trials, 7 models. Mean share of numeric confidences at 95% or more: 91.7% (range 72.4-96.8%). 7 of 7 Invalid on numeric confidence. Token log-prob predicted verbalized confidence at cross-validated R2 below 0.01. Categorical format: six of seven models fell below 5% accuracy. In the reasoning-distilled model, trace length correlated -.36 with confidence (p<.001).
limits: Q5_K_M quantised, greedy decoding, minimal prompt, 3-9B only. Authors say this does not mean internal signals are absent.
agent_relevance: Test for saturation before using any stated number: if most outputs sit at one value, the number carries no information.

source: Zhao et al. (2026, COLM) Wired for Overconfidence: A Mechanistic Perspective on Inflated Verbalized Confidence
finding: A small set of MLP blocks and attention heads in middle-to-late layers writes the inflation signal for verbalized confidence. Targeted inference-time intervention on those circuits improves calibration.
numbers: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct across three datasets. Top 3,000 edges out of 527,743 (Qwen) and 693,267 (Llama) form a sufficient sub-circuit (under 0.6% of edges).
limits: Needs weights; 3B models only.
agent_relevance: Not usable in a prompt scaffold, but supports the claim that overconfidence is systematic and can be fixed by an outside correction.

source: Ou et al. (2025) BrowseConf: Confidence-Guided Test-Time Scaling for Web Agents
finding: In long web-search agent runs, stated confidence is too high yet still ranks answers: near zero accuracy at low stated confidence, more than double average accuracy above 95%. The authors retry until confidence passes a threshold. This used fewer tokens than a fixed budget at similar accuracy.
numbers: gpt-oss-120b and DeepSeek-V3.1 on BrowseComp. DeepSeek-V3.1 in the 90-94% confidence bin had only 53.33% accuracy at best. Its score with confidence elicited was 30.49% vs 30.0% reported, so eliciting confidence does not hurt. Threshold chosen on a validation set (SailorFog-QA).
limits: Open agentic models. Token-saving numbers not extracted from the tables this session. Calibration is poor; the signal is ordinal only.
agent_relevance: Closest match to a use inside an agent loop: stated confidence as a stop/retry gate, with the threshold set on held-out data, not the model's face value (G3).

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Agentic Uncertainty Quantification (AUQ)
finding: Dual-process agent method: verbalized confidence and its explanation are kept in memory (System 1), and a reflection step fires only when confidence is low (System 2). Gains in success rate and trajectory-level calibration on ALFWorld, WebShop and a deep-research benchmark.
numbers: Success-rate gains of +10.7% (ALFWorld) and +13.6% (WebShop, 42.5% SR) over the baseline in the text. Corrects 14.3% of ReAct's failures and regresses 3.6% of its successes. ReAct shows severe miscalibration on the minimum-step reliability metric.
limits: Frontier models (GPT-5.1, GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5, Qwen3, DeepSeek-V3.1). Single paper; the ensemble baseline is CoT-SC.
agent_relevance: A tested example of G1 inside a loop: reflect only when stated confidence is low. Memory of earlier confidence can stop blind carry-over.

source: Hathidara (2026) Can an Agent Learn to Predict Its Own Failure? Outcome-Grounded Confidence Calibration in LLM Agents
finding: Step-level verbalized confidence of an acting agent starts near chance for predicting the episode outcome. RL with proper-scoring rewards against the eventual outcome lifts it, and selective execution improves without hurting task success.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B agent in ALFWorld, TextWorld, WebShop. Offline: AUROC rises from near chance to 0.68-0.85; the top 10% most confident steps succeed 4.3x more often than average. Online on ALFWorld: ECE from 0.42 to below 0.12.
limits: Small model with RL. The trained agent knows early which tasks it will fail, but telling a good from a bad attempt at the same task is harder.
agent_relevance: Per-step stated confidence is weak untrained. Score it against episode outcomes, not step correctness.
